why: The statement names two Hardy–Littlewood statements: an odd-order critical zero in every (T,T+T^(1/4+ε)], and an odd-order count ≥ cH for H = T^(1/2+ε). No post-snapshot event reaches either. Alpöge–Furman and Lamzouri prove proportions of simple critical zeros averaged over (T,2T], a different quantity, so they are variants. Claude's generated role is recorded but does not bear on this problem. Wang's short-interval theorem works only for θ > 0.5501, which is above both exponents, and counts simple zeros, so it is also a variant. I scored the ChatGPT-6 Astra quote ('implement the ideas of the proof') as assisted, but it does not matter because the event is discarded. The close call is the pre-2024 literature. Secondary sources say Hardy–Littlewood 1921 already proved both statements. Karatsuba 1984 gives part 2 by splitting intervals, and Karatsuba 1981 and Moser 1976 reportedly give part 1. The record only has these through summaries, and the Wikipedia article itself calls them conjectures. So I scored each as a case rather than whole, which keeps the problem open rather than open_stale.
doubts: Several secondary reports say Hardy–Littlewood 1921 proved both statements outright. If the primary text confirms that, hardy-littlewood-1921 should be whole and the problem open_stale. The January 2024 wording of the Wikipedia article was not retrieved. 'Implement the ideas' in Wang's v1 is ambiguous, and v2 softens it.
